summary: Specifies the TCP Authentication Option (TCP-AO), which replaces the TCP MD5 Signature option of RFC 2385. It supports stronger message authentication codes, protects against replay on long-lived connections, and works with static or externally managed keys. It suits uses like BGP and LDP. It is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: TCP-AO lets two TCP endpoints check that segments came from an endpoint with the right key and were not changed in transit. It supports key changes and replay protection, but another process must establish and manage the keys.

questions: how does tcp-ao prevent replay attacks
subtitle: Authenticate TCP segments and coordinate key changes without changing TCP itself.

tldr.problem: TCP MD5 provides limited algorithm choice and no built-in way to coordinate key changes or prevent replay on long-lived connections.
tldr.mechanism: TCP-AO adds a TCP option carrying key identifiers and a message authentication code, with per-connection traffic keys and sequence extensions.
tldr.outcome: TCP-AO obsoletes RFC 2385 and supports IPv4 and IPv6, but key management and algorithm negotiation remain external to TCP-AO.

today: RFC 5925 is a Proposed Standard and obsoletes RFC 2385. It recommends TCP-AO as the replacement while allowing TCP MD5 for connections to legacy peers.

sections.title: Replacing TCP MD5
sections.content:
TCP MD5 was used to protect long-lived TCP connections, including routing-protocol sessions, but it tied authentication to one algorithm and did not define key management. RFC 5925 replaces it with the TCP Authentication Option (TCP-AO).

TCP-AO can use multiple message authentication code (MAC) algorithms, coordinate a move between keys, and derive different traffic keys for each connection. It does not encrypt data or replace IPsec/IKE.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP-AO updates TCP's older authentication option. It lets endpoints change keys and choose supported authentication algorithms, while leaving key setup to an external method.

sections.title: Fields in the TCP-AO Option
sections.content:
The option uses TCP Kind 29 and contains a length, a KeyID, an RNextKeyID, and a variable-length MAC. KeyID identifies the master key tuple used for this segment; RNextKeyID tells the other endpoint which receive key is ready for later segments.

A TCP connection MUST NOT use TCP-AO and TCP MD5 at the same time. A segment must contain no more than one TCP-AO option, and its length must fit the TCP header.
sections.plainLanguage: Each protected segment carries identifiers for the key in use and the next key the sender is ready to receive. The MAC lets the receiver check the segment's protected contents.

sections.title: Master Keys and Connection Keys
sections.content:
A Master Key Tuple (MKT) associates a master key with a TCP socket pair, key identifiers, a key-derivation function, and a MAC algorithm. The MKT derives directional traffic keys for individual TCP connections.

The derivation uses the IP addresses, port numbers, and the connection's Initial Sequence Numbers. This makes traffic keys distinct across repeated connections that reuse a socket pair. The MKT itself is configured or managed outside TCP-AO.
sections.plainLanguage: A shared master key is not used directly for every segment. TCP-AO derives separate keys for each connection and direction from the key and connection details.

sections.title: What the MAC Protects
sections.content:
The MAC covers the Sequence Number Extension, the IP pseudoheader, the TCP header, and TCP data. The TCP checksum and the TCP-AO MAC field are set to zero for the calculation. A configuration flag controls whether other TCP options are included.

TCP-AO does not provide confidentiality. Its MAC detects changes and helps authenticate a segment to a receiver that has the matching key.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver checks a MAC over the packet's addresses, TCP information, and data. The option authenticates and checks integrity; it does not hide the data.

sections.title: Key Changes and Replay Protection
sections.content:
The KeyID and RNextKeyID fields coordinate use of new MKTs so a sender can wait until the receiver is ready. The endpoints arrange new keys out of band; TCP-AO does not negotiate or remove keys by itself.

TCP sequence numbers can wrap on a long-lived connection. TCP-AO adds a 32-bit Sequence Number Extension (SNE) to distinguish repeated sequence numbers and include that distinction in the MAC.
sections.plainLanguage: Two key identifiers help endpoints switch to a key both sides have prepared. An extra sequence-number part helps distinguish old segments from later segments after TCP's sequence numbers wrap.
